item.title: How to Think for Yourself Using the Grit–Grace Scale
item.description:
Boundaries

How to Think for Yourself Using the Grit–Grace Scale

Build self-authority to navigate uncertainty when life offers no clear answers.

Posted July 19, 2026

Key points
  • Low self-trust leads us to self-abandon and outsource our judgment to experts, trends, and formulas.
  • Psychological adulthood means discerning when grit, grace, or both best fit the moment.
  • Self-trust grows through reflection on values, capacity, sustainability, and real-world patterns.
What do I need?
Source: Darius Bashar/2020

We are drowning in psychological advice while simultaneously starving for our own self-authority. Influencers, authors, and well-meaning experts are constantly telling us how to set boundaries, how to forgive, when to walk away, and what it really looks like to “do the work.” Yet in nearly every therapy room I sit in, I hear a quieter, more unsettling concern:

“But how do I know what the right decision is for me?”

In our fear of getting it wrong, and of being responsible for that outcome, we often turn outward for certainty. This can be the natural consequence of growing up in adversity or environments that taught us to doubt our perceptions. When everyone has an opinion about your life, it can feel safer to follow rules than to trust your own voice.

Losing Your Inner Authority

In my clinical work, I often see how deeply people grieve what they never received. No explanation, justification, or “I did my best” can soften the ache of realizing that something essential was missing—needs such as a sense of being emotionally safe, supported, encouraged, and truly seen. In this way, grief is not only about loss. It is about awareness.

It is the moment you stop explaining away what was missing and begin naming what you needed. And awareness changes your role in your life. As you grieve what you did not receive, you also realize that you are now responsible for how you choose to meet those needs. However difficult the realization, it is also the beginning of self-authority and self-trust.

What is happening within individuals is also happening culturally. We live in an era saturated with advice from influencers, programs, and psychological frameworks that promise the “right” way to live. While such resources have their place, they also train many of us to look outward for certainty instead of inward to discern which choices align with our values. We are increasingly aware, yet profoundly unsure how to trust our own decision-making.

I encourage clients to use guidance from others as “tools, not rules.” Boundaries, communication, forgiveness, therapy, reflection—these are perspectives to consider, not mandates for how you must respond in order to be “doing it right.” When advice becomes a rulebook, self-trust quietly erodes. We stop looking inward for our own answers and begin looking outward for direction on what we are "supposed" to do

The Grit–Grace Scale

Without a secure sense of self-authority, uncertainty worsens psychological distress. Relying on the advice of experts feels safer than using our own discernment because it spares us the challenge of choosing. We want a map, a formula, a clear right answer. But when we outsource our need for answers, we abandon the very wisdom we are meant to develop. Following the advice of others is not how we grow in self-trust.

This is where I introduce a framework I call the Grit–Grace Scale.

This framework is a useful navigation guide for whenever life asks us to choose—whether to set firmer boundaries or soften them, to push forward or pause, to speak up or stay quiet, to persist or pivot, to repair or release, to hold steady or let go. It invites a deeper developmental question: What is healthy for me in this season of my life? And what does that require from me?

On one end of the spectrum lies grit—the courage to protect yourself, to set firm boundaries, to walk away when necessary. Grit honors dignity, safety, and self-respect. There are moments when grit is what restores your dignity. It is the strength that says “enough.” It draws lines where there have been none. It refuses to abandon the self for the comfort of belonging. Grit is the voice that asks: What does my integrity require of me right now? Here, dignity and clarity take precedence over harmony.

On the other end lies grace—the openness to remain curious, to hold complexity, and to stay receptive to growth and repair. Grace honors humanity, compassion, and the possibility of repair or growth. Grace is the capacity to remain curious instead of defensive, to soften without collapsing, to allow for complexity and human limitation. Grace asks different questions: Where can I remain open without betraying myself? Grace helps us refine boundaries.

Psychological adulthood is not choosing one side forever. It is learning to move between them with discernment.

How Do You Know What You Need?

This is the question people always ask next, and it is the heart of self-trust.

Discernment is an internal inventory regulated by identity-linked values. Here are four key areas of reflection that can help clarify what is actually happening and how you want to respond to it.

1. Integrity Alignment: What would it take to act from my values rather than my fear?

  • Consider acting not to avoid conflict, but to protect your dignity and the person you are becoming.

2. Nervous System Capacity: What can my body realistically tolerate right now?

  • Even the “right” choice is not right if your system is constantly braced, frozen, or overwhelmed.

3. Energetic Sustainability: Can I keep living this way without losing myself?

  • If your life requires you to shrink, silence, or abandon parts of who you are, your system is already giving you the answer.

4. Relational Reality: What is actually happening (as opposed to what I hope is happening)?

  • Discernment looks at patterns, not promises. It's about accountability, not intention.

Together, these questions show you how much grit you need, how much grace you can afford, and what your system can realistically sustain.

Where Real Inner-Authority Begins

Inner-authority is not about perfect compliance or choosing the “right” philosophy. It is about becoming the kind of adult who can reflect honestly, tolerate uncertainty, and take responsibility for their own choices. Yes, even when the answers are not simple.

We need more adults who are willing to trust their own discernment and build their lives from it.
